title: Telling a Story
description: Turn the past tense you already have into a story: set the scene with كان, keep the listener hooked with لما and فجأة, and land the ending. The irregular verbs a Sanaa storyteller cannot do without.
approach: GPA Phase 3–4 — story-based. The learner hears a two-minute anecdote twice, rebuilds it from picture prompts, then tells their own with the same skeleton.
unlock_condition: Retell the six-picture story with at least four of the six events in order, using كان at least once
can_do: Tell what happened, setting the scene with 'was' + a verb
Sequence events with 'while', 'suddenly' and 'in the end'
Use the most common irregular past verbs in Ṣanʿāni

grammar.title: كان sets the scene; the short verbs move the story
grammar.explanation: A Sanaa story opens with كان: كان الجو بارد 'the weather was cold', كنت في السوق 'I was in the market'. Put كان in front of a present-tense verb and you get 'was doing' or 'used to': كنت أمشي 'I was walking', كان يسير كل يوم 'he used to go every day'. Then the events come in the plain past: فجأة وقع، ضحكنا، في الآخر لقيناه. Watch the short verbs — the ones whose middle letter is a long vowel or whose last letter is ي: سار becomes سرت 'I went', قال becomes قلت, شاف becomes شفت, and لقى / نسي / حكى become لقيت / نسيت / حكيت with the ي turning into -ii-. Say the story once with كان at the start and the short verbs doing the rest and it already sounds Yemeni.

examples.arabic: كنت أمشي في السوق ولقيت صاحبي
examples.english: I was walking in the market and I found my friend
He used to go to the qat session every day
I forgot the key at home
He told us a story and we all laughed

examples.arabic: ما كانش فيه أحد في البيت

culture.title: The story is the currency of the mafraj
culture.note: In a Sanaa sitting room the afternoon runs on stories, and a good one is worth more than the qat. The teller exaggerates — ten people become a hundred, a fright becomes near death — and nobody checks the facts. What is expected of you as a listener is noise: والله؟ 'really?', لا! 'no!', a loud laugh at the punchline and تصدّق؟ 'would you believe it?' thrown back. Sitting silent reads as boredom. When it is your turn, start with مرة 'one time…' and end with في الآخر so people know the punchline has landed.

phrases.english: Would you believe it? I had no idea
One time I was in Old Sanaa…

vocabulary.teaching_note: The scene-setter of every story. كنت (I was / you were), كانت (she was), كانو (they were). Before a present verb it means 'was doing' or 'used to'. It also carries the past of 'there is': كان فيه.
vocabulary.image_scene: An old photo in a frame on a mafraj cushion, sepia, a hand pointing at it.

example.arabic: كنت في عدن السنة اللي فاتت
example.transliteration: kunt fi ʿadan is-sana lli faatat
example.english: I was in Aden last year

vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger recounting yesterday; كان / كنت opening the narration.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The natural Yemeni 'when / while' for narration — لما وصلت 'when I arrived', لما كنت أطبخ 'while I was cooking'. Not a question word: for 'when?' you already have متى. Never بينما.
vocabulary.image_scene: Split frame: a woman stirring a pot on the left, a door opening on the right, an arrow between them.

example.english: While I was cooking, the guests came

vocabulary.video_hint: Any anecdote with two overlapping events; لما marks the background one.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The word that makes everybody look up. Said with a pause before it and a jump in the voice. Spelled فجأة, often typed فجاه online.
vocabulary.image_scene: A cat leaping out of a cardboard box, a startled man dropping his tea glass.
vocabulary.video_hint: Prank and comedy clips; the narrator's فجأة right before the twist.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ق is g in Sanaa, so giṣṣa. حكاية is also used for a tale. 'Tell me the story' is احكي لي القصة.
vocabulary.image_scene: An open storybook on a carpet, a small lamp, a grandmother's hands.

example.english: Tell me the story from the beginning

vocabulary.video_hint: Storytime vlogs titled قصة / قصتي; the word said in the intro.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ايش حصل؟ 'what happened?' is how every story is invited. صار is heard too and means the same; حصل is the safer default in Sanaa.
vocabulary.image_scene: A broken vase on a floor, two people looking at it with raised hands.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone asking ايش حصل on seeing a mess or a shocked face.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Told a story' is حكى, not قال — قال reports words, حكى tells the whole thing. حكى لي 'he told me', حكيت له 'I told him'. Weak verb: the final ى becomes -ii- when you add a suffix.
vocabulary.image_scene: An older man gesturing mid-story to three listeners on floor cushions.

example.arabic: حكى لي كل شي حصل في العرس
example.transliteration: ḥaka li kull shi ḥaṣal fil-ʿurs
example.english: He told me everything that happened at the wedding

vocabulary.video_hint: A creator saying احكي لكم / حكى لي before an anecdote.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Yemeni 'find' — ق is g: liga, ligiit 'I found'. Also 'met, came across'. ما لقيتش 'I didn't find (it)'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand lifting a cushion to reveal a phone underneath, relief on a face.

example.english: I found the phone under the chair

vocabulary.video_hint: Searching for something, then لقيته with the object held up.

vocabulary.teaching_note: نسيت 'I forgot' is one of the most-used past verbs in any dialect. Weak verb like لقى: nisiit, nisyat 'she forgot'. Good stories start with a forgotten key.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man outside a locked door patting his empty pockets.

example.english: I forgot the key inside the house

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone realising they left something; نسيت said with a hand on the forehead.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ذ is a real dh in Sanaa — tadhakkar, not tazakkar. تذكرت 'I remembered', تتذكر؟ 'do you remember?' opens a shared memory.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman with a finger raised and a lightbulb glow, an old wedding photo beside her.

example.english: Do you remember when we went to Hodeidah?

vocabulary.video_hint: Friends reminiscing; تتذكر لما… opening a shared story.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The reaction every story wants. ضحكنا 'we laughed', ضحّكني 'he made me laugh'. ض is the emphatic d.
vocabulary.image_scene: Three men in a mafraj doubled over laughing, one slapping his knee.

example.english: We laughed until our stomachs hurt

vocabulary.video_hint: Comedy channels; the crew laughing and the word ضحك in reaction.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A participle: كنت خايف 'I was afraid'. Feminine خايفة, plural خايفين. خايف من 'afraid of'. Storytellers exaggerate it: كنت خايف موت 'scared to death'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A boy hiding behind a door, eyes wide, a dark hallway beyond.

example.english: I was afraid of the dog

vocabulary.video_hint: Prank reactions; the victim saying خفت / كنت خايف afterwards.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Signals the punchline is coming. Also بالآخر and آخر شي 'the last thing'. Learners often reach for MSA أخيراً — say في الآخر.
vocabulary.image_scene: A finish line with a small flag; a relieved man crossing it.

example.english: In the end we found the car

vocabulary.video_hint: The wrap-up of any anecdote; في الآخر before the resolution.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Half of all funny stories involve someone falling. وقعت 'I fell', وقع من فوق 'he fell from above'. Also 'it fell' for objects.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man slipping on a wet step, tea glass flying.

example.english: He fell in the street and people were laughing

vocabulary.video_hint: Fail compilations narrated in Yemeni; وقع at the fall.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The exit from every scare story. هربت 'I ran away', هربو 'they fled'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A cat sprinting out of a kitchen, a woman with a broom behind it.

example.english: He saw the dog and ran away

vocabulary.video_hint: Prank clips where the target bolts; هرب in the voiceover.

vocabulary.teaching_note: صرخت 'I screamed' — the moment of the story where the teller raises their voice to act it out.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman with hands up mid-scream, a cockroach on the wall.

example.english: I screamed and the whole neighbourhood heard

vocabulary.video_hint: Reaction and scare clips; صرخ / صرخت in the retelling.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The storyteller's hook and the listener's reaction in one word. ق is g: tṣaddag. To a woman تصدّقي, to a group تصدّقو.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man leaning in with raised eyebrows and an open palm, mid-sentence.

example.english: Would you believe it? The dog came home by itself

vocabulary.video_hint: Comedy hosts addressing the camera with تصدقوا before a reveal.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The emotional turn of a story: زعل مني 'he got upset with me'. زعلان is the state 'upset'. Not quite anger — that comes in Lesson 4.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man with crossed arms turning his face away from a friend.

example.arabic: زعلت مني لأني نسيت عيد ميلادها
example.transliteration: ziʿlat minni laʾanni nisiit ʿiid miilaadha
example.english: She got upset with me because I forgot her birthday

vocabulary.video_hint: Family skits; someone sulking as زعل / زعلان is said.

dialogue.speaker: Ali

sound_spotlight.example: لقى → لقيت، نسي → نسيت، حكى → حكيت
sound_spotlight.explanation: When the last letter is ى and you add a suffix, it becomes a long -ii-: ligiit, nisiit, ḥakiit. Hold the ii; a short i sounds like a different verb.

sound_spotlight.sound: ق → g in liga, giṣṣa, tṣaddag
sound_spotlight.explanation: Story words are full of ق, and in Sanaa every one is a hard g — even in words a learner met as q in class.
The stress moves to the suffix syllable when you add -t: kátab 'he wrote' but katábt 'I wrote'. Listeners use the stress, not just the ending, to hear who did it.

lesson_sequence.detail: The learner hears Hamood's dog story once at full speed with pictures only. One question: did he find the key?
The 18 words on cards, each with its example sentence and audio; كان and the weak verbs get a second card showing the suffixed forms.
The anecdote replayed line by line; كان + verb lines highlighted in one colour, the plain past events in another. The learner taps which is scene and which is event.
Six pictures out of order; the learner drags them into sequence and records one sentence per picture, guided by لما / فجأة / في الآخر prompts.
Short audio bursts of a story pause; the learner picks and says the fitting reaction: والله؟ / لا! / تصدّق؟ / hahaha.
Record a 30-second story about something you forgot or lost, using كان once and three connectors. The AI checks tense and connectors.
Word counter rolls up; nudge to tell the same story to a Yemeni friend and count their reactions.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you are with Yemeni friends, ask ايش حصل؟ about their day and react out loud at least three times.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on lesson complete. Activates حصل and the listener reactions.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tell someone the story of the last thing you forgot or lost. Start with مرة كنت… and end with في الآخر.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification two days later. Production of the full skeleton.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Watch a Yemeni comedy sketch and write down every فجأة and لما you hear.
real_world_prompts.context: Video-companion prompt; recognition of the connectors in fast speech.

video_needs.scene: Someone recounting an anecdote to camera or friends in a mafraj; a prank with the victim retelling what happened afterwards; laughter and reactions audible.
